Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  - Left elbow swelling noticed approximately 1 week ago while in the shower.
  - No recalled trauma or injury; desk-based job.
  - Warm to touch; feels like there is fluid inside; not painful; full range of motion.
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  - Onset ~1 week prior; patient states it “feels a bit better now.”
- ENT symptoms (as applicable):
  - Not reported in this consultation: throat swelling/closure sensation, voice change, dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling, nasal/ocular symptoms, stridor/noisy breathing, dyspnea, distribution of swelling (lips/tongue/uvula/face), ear or neck symptoms.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  - No prior similar elbow swelling reported.
  - Past medical history: osteoarthritis diagnosed by a GP years ago (no further details provided).
  - No prior hospital care or injection therapy for this issue documented.
- Allergies and current medications:
  - Allergies: Peanut allergy (details of reaction severity not documented). No known drug allergies reported.
  - Current medications: None regularly.
  - New treatment advised today: Ibuprofen 400 mg twice daily; route not documented; advised to take after food and stop if heartburn occurs.
- Any relevant social context:
  - Runs 2–3 times per week; otherwise healthy and active. Works at a desk. No mention of accompaniment/supervision.

Objective:
- Observable swelling and distribution:
  - Video inspection of left elbow: visible swelling with localized warmth. Skin over tip noted to be dry. Minimal tenderness adjacent to the swelling. Full movement preserved.
- Airway/breathing descriptors:
  - Not recorded.
- Mental status and associated features:
  - Not recorded.
- Vitals and examination findings:
  - Not recorded.
- Presence of another person with the patient:
  - Not recorded.

Assessment:
- Suspected left olecranon bursitis.
- Septic arthritis considered unlikely at present.
- Justification: Atraumatic onset ~1 week, warm localized swelling with minimal tenderness and preserved range of motion on video exam; patient reports no significant pain and slight improvement. No systemic or airway/ENT red flags discussed.

Plan:
- Immediate actions taken/advised:
  - Begin ibuprofen 400 mg twice daily (route not documented); take after food; stop if heartburn occurs; over-the-counter.
  - Order blood tests via mailed forms: inflammatory markers, infection screen, rheumatologic antibodies, and gout assessment.
- Instructions to patient:
  - Forms will be mailed with instructions on where to have blood drawn. Results expected ~5–6 days after sampling.
  - Arrange follow-up (phone/video or in-person) after blood tests to review results and reassess the elbow.
- Escalation criteria/red flags:
  - If the elbow becomes very red, very painful, or the redness spreads/becomes more intense, “get on the phone or have a video appointment with one of us as soon as possible,” as this may require urgent assessment/treatment for possible septic arthritis.
- Follow-up:
  - Follow-up appointment to review labs and re-examine joint after tests are completed.
- ENT-specific:
  - No ENT symptoms or interventions addressed during this visit.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements for an acute ENT/allergy presentation:
  - No ENT symptom review (throat tightness, voice change, dysphagia, dyspnea, facial/oral swelling) documented.
  - Airway assessment not documented.
  - Severity and specifics of peanut allergy reactions not documented; epinephrine auto-injector ownership/use not documented.
  - No vitals recorded.
- Internal conflicts:
  - None noted in the transcript.
- Transcript quality:
  - Generally clear; minor filler words. Video inspection of the elbow performed; no technical issues affecting clinical content.
